analysis.one_liner: Bans most noncompete agreements that block workers from taking a new job.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to ban most noncompete agreements, covering an estimated 1 in 5 U.S. workers, was referred to the Senate labor committee and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for employers to make workers sign noncompete agreements, which forbid employees from going to work for a competitor or starting a rival business after they leave. Employers could still protect trade secrets and use nondisclosure agreements, and there are narrow exceptions for someone selling a business or a departing partner. The Federal Trade Commission and the Department of Labor would both enforce the ban, and workers could sue for damages.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers bound by noncompete agreements, which economists cited in the bill estimate cover 1 in 5 American workers. Banning them would let workers change jobs freely, which research links to higher wages and faster career growth. It would also help new businesses and competitors trying to hire experienced people.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any person from entering into, enforcing, or threatening to enforce a noncompete agreement with a worker; such agreements would have no force or effect.
Congress's own findings state that economists estimate 1 in 5 workers is covered by a noncompete agreement, and that such agreements reduce wages, restrict worker mobility, and slow innovation.

Enforcement comes from two directions: the Federal Trade Commission treats violations as unfair or deceptive practices, and the Department of Labor can investigate complaints and sue violators, with civil fines of up to $5,000 per week paid to the aggrieved worker.
Workers get a private right of action in federal court, with actual damages plus attorney's fees and costs if they win.

Employers keep narrower tools: the bill explicitly preserves nondisclosure agreements and trade secret protections, which the bill's findings call adequate protection for customer lists and confidential information.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who use noncompete agreements to keep trained workers from leaving or joining competitors. They would lose a tool for retaining staff and suppressing turnover, and would face fines or lawsuits if they kept enforcing such agreements. They would retain trade secret and nondisclosure protections instead.

drawbacks.text: The ban applies only to noncompete agreements entered into after the law takes effect; agreements already signed would not be voided, so many of the 1 in 5 covered workers would see no immediate relief.

The exceptions favor those already at the top: owners who sell a business, departing partners, and senior executives with severance packages worth at least a year of pay can still sign noncompetes, while rank-and-file employees cannot.

Employers argue noncompetes protect their investment in training and confidential information; the bill answers this by preserving trade secret and nondisclosure law, but an employer losing a trained employee to a competitor would still bear the cost of that training with no contractual protection.
Splitting enforcement between the FTC and the Department of Labor, with shared standards due just 90 days after enactment, could create confusion about which agency handles which complaint.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains for workers are substantial and the costs to employers are modest, because employers keep narrower, better-targeted tools like trade secret law and nondisclosure agreements. The main design weakness is that it leaves existing noncompete agreements in place and carves out executives and business sellers, so the workers most likely to benefit are ordinary employees, which is also where the agreements do the most wage damage.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on February 25, 2021, read twice, and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Chris Murphy introduced the bill on February 25, 2021 with three cosponsors: Sens. Todd Young and Kevin Cramer, both Republicans, and Sen. Tim Kaine, a Democrat.
The same day it was introduced, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The committee took no further action on the bill; no hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded for the rest of the 117th Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died without ever coming to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on noncompete agreements came out ahead: the ban never advanced, so they kept the ability to bind roughly 1 in 5 workers, including low- and mid-wage employees, to restrictions on changing jobs. No member ever had to vote on the record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from day one: two Democrats (Murphy, Kaine) and two Republicans (Young, Cramer) backed it, and no senator is recorded as opposing it, but the committee never moved it, so there were no roll calls to measure the split.

industries.industry: Employers that use noncompete agreements (spanning retail, food service, staffing, tech, and healthcare)
industries.note: These employers use noncompetes to stop employees, including low- and mid-wage workers, from leaving for a competitor, which the bill's findings say suppresses wages and restricts worker mobility. The ban would remove that tool, though they would keep trade secret and nondisclosure protections.

industries.industry: Business sellers, departing partners, and senior executives with severance packages
industries.note: The bill's exceptions let business sellers, partners in a dissolving partnership, and top executives with a year's worth of severance keep signing noncompetes, so this group loses nothing.
